articles.title: oPt: UNRWA Situation Report #237 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
articles.description: Please refer to the attached files. Highlights The Gaza Strip On 12 October, UNRWA opened a new health facility in Jabalia and began receiving patients. As UNRWA’s northernmost health facility in the Gaza Strip, the clinic expands access to health services for underserved communities. Together with the Saftawi Health Centre, the two facilities provide new anchor points for delivering health services to thousands of Palestine Refugees in the area. UNRWA recorded several significant armed incidents affecting its facilities and schools-turned-shelters. At least six displaced people, including a child, were injured and one person was killed while sheltering inside UNRWA facilities, mostly as a result of stray bullets. Operations at several facilities across Rafah, Khan Younis and the Middle Area were also temporarily suspended, either due to insecurity or following evacuation orders issued by Israeli forces. UNRWA’s winterisation response is underway, with winter emergency teams activated across all areas to clean manholes, gullies, and drainage networks, identify high-risk locations, inspect available equipment, and put preventive measures in place, including sandbags in flood-prone areas. Winterisation preparedness, however, remains seriously constrained by limited operational capacity: many pumps to address flooding are not functioning due to lack of engine oil and spare parts, and heavy machinery cannot enter Gaza. The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem Marking three years since the attacks of 7 October 2023, movement and access re-strictions were tightened across the occupied West Bank. The olive harvest season officially commenced on 15 October, accompanied by settler violence and access restrictions impacting Palestinian farmers in several areas of the occupied West Bank. During the reporting period, one Palestinian was reportedly killed in an incident related to settler violence. Key Points Fatalities and injuries Between 7 October 2023 and 9 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the Health Cluster, 74,370 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 175,371 were injured. This includes 1,481 fatalities and 5,410 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 9 October 2026. UNRWA has recorded 394 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 83 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2], as of 20 October. Health crisis Hypothermia remains a serious risk, particularly for newborns and infants, with deaths reported in previous winters since the war began. UNRWA health and nutrition teams are strengthening counselling for women and caregivers on breastfeeding, skin-to-skin care and other simple measures to keep children warm. Infant warming units are being distributed across UNRWA health facilities to address emergency cases. However, supply restrictions have prevented the entry of additional warmers for community distribution, while use of existing units depends on unreliable electricity supplies. In September, six UNRWA health centres also experienced temporary disruptions due to overloaded generators having to be switched off until new lubricant oil can be found. This highlights the growing operational impact of the shortage of fuel, lubricant oil, and spare parts on the delivery of healthcare. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in September, 84 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene. Water insecurity thus remains a significant concern, despite signs of improvement (91 per cent of the population reported water insecurity in the previous round). Access to basic hygiene supplies also remained severely constrained, with 89 per cent of households reporting insufficient access to essential hygiene items. Displacement, site management UNRWA continues to monitor the movement of displaced persons and displacement sites. A total of 113 UNRWA collective emergency shelters host 65,000 internally displaced persons. Shelter needs According to the Shelter Cluster’s classification, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks. Operational implications and humanitarian response Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with more than 4,000 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, health, and other services to Palestine Refugees. All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[3] that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact between Israeli officials and UNRWA. Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including the Gaza Strip, since the end of January 2025. Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people. According to OCHA, between 7 October 2023 and 9 October 2026, 1,143 Palestinians – at least 250 of them children – were killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Ninety-six of them have been killed since the beginning of 2026. Marking three years since the attacks of 7 October 2023, movement and access re-strictions were tightened across the occupied West Bank. Settler violence and harassment continued to account for a significant percentage of recorded protection incidents, with 395 incidents and at least 115 related injuries reported from 7-20 October alone. In addition to widespread reports of obstruction and attacks targeting the olive harvest, sustained pressure on Palestinian communities is contributing to an increasingly coercive environment and heightened protection concerns. A Palestinian from Burqa was reportedly killed in the context of settler violence on 7 October. Other Palestinians sustained injuries during the incident. The incident underscores the high levels of settler violence currently affecting Palestinian communities, particularly during the olive harvest season. On 10 October, a Palestinian from Beit Ula was shot and killed by Israeli forces using live ammunition in Hebron City. Israeli forces have continued to keep all entrances to Madama village closed since 11 October. The olive harvest season officially commenced on 15 October, accompanied by settler violence and access restrictions impacting Palestinian farmers in several areas of the West Bank. On 16 October, in Abu Falah, a foreign journalist was among the injured. On 17 October, in At-Tayba, a European diplomatic delegation came under attack during a visit to observe the olive harvest.

articles.title: Lebanon Complex Emergency, Operation update #5 (MDRLB017)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. A. SITUATION ANALYSIS Description of the crisis Lebanon entered 2026 facing a protracted and multidimensional crisis shaped by the cumulative effects of the financial and economic collapse that began in 2019, the consequences of successive rounds of hostilities since October 2023, large-scale population displacement, weakened public services and infrastructure, and persistent institutional and financial constraints. While the country had begun to show signs of economic stabilization and recovery during 2025, the renewed escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026 abruptly reversed this trajectory and generated a new large-scale humanitarian emergency. The World Bank estimates that the renewed conflict derailed Lebanon’s fragile recovery and projects the economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026, further constraining household purchasing power, livelihoods, public finances and the capacity of already overstretched institutions and services to respond to humanitarian needs. The renewed escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026 triggered large-scale displacement across Lebanon, with more than 1.2 million people forced to flee their homes at the height of the crisis. Many displaced families sought refuge in collective shelters, including public schools and other facilities, while others stayed with host families or in temporary accommodation. By 13 April, approximately 140,914 people were accommodated in 684 collective shelters. As the intensity of hostilities gradually decreased, displacement patterns shifted, with increasing numbers of families returning to their areas of origin and a progressive reduction in collective shelter occupancy. By 24 June, the number of people residing in collective shelters had decreased to 80,611 across 584 sites, while 523,249 people had returned to their communities. This trend continued over the following months, alongside the gradual closure and consolidation of collective shelters, particularly those established in public schools ahead of the new academic year. As of 29 September, IOM recorded 329,686 internally displaced persons, including 14,277 people in 154 collective sites, while 877,203 people had returned to their areas of origin. Despite the substantial return movements, conditions in many affected areas remained challenging. Extensive damage to residential buildings and essential infrastructure left many households unable to return to their homes, while others returned to partially damaged properties or areas where basic services remained disrupted. Continued airstrikes and security incidents, particularly in southern Lebanon, alongside explosive ordnance risks and limited livelihood opportunities, further constrained safe and sustainable returns. Consequently, significant shelter and early recovery needs persisted among displaced and returning populations, despite the overall reduction in displacement figures. According to the Ministry of Public Health, as of 10 September 2026, 4,383 people had been killed and 12,406 injured since the renewed escalation began on 2 March. The crisis has unfolded alongside broader and increasingly complex population movements. Lebanon continues to host a large refugee population, while movements between Lebanon and Syria have increased amid changing conditions in both countries and wider regional instability. The 2026 Lebanon Response Plan estimates that approximately 1.12 million displaced Syrians are living in Lebanon. Return movements to Syria have taken place alongside continued arrivals and internal movements, creating a complex protection environment involving Lebanese communities, refugees, migrants, internally displaced people and returnees. The renewed conflict has also exacerbated Lebanon’s existing food security and socioeconomic crisis. The April 2026 IPC update estimated that approximately 1.24 million people, or 24 per cent of the analysed population, would face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between April and August 2026, compared with 874,000 people between November 2025 and March 2026. By 30 September, UNICEF reported that four in five surveyed households were struggling to afford basic necessities, demonstrating the extent to which renewed conflict has compounded years of socioeconomic deterioration and depleted household coping capacities. Public services and infrastructure have also sustained significant impacts. Health facilities and ambulances have been affected by attacks, while insecurity and damage have disrupted access to health care. By June 2026, the Ministry of Public Health reported that 17 hospitals had been damaged, including three that were forced to close. Since the renewed escalation began, 133 healthcare workers had been killed and 402 injured, while 172 attacks on emergency medical service vehicles and stations had been recorded. The education sector has similarly been affected and that among 1,089 education facilities assessed, 436 were damaged and 37 destroyed. Damage and disruption to water, sanitation, electricity, housing and other essential infrastructure have further constrained access to basic services in affected and return areas. By the end of September 2026, the situation had evolved from the peak phase of mass displacement towards a complex combination of continued humanitarian response, population return and early recovery. However, the security situation remained volatile, with ongoing attacks and airstrikes, particularly in southern Lebanon, continuing to result in casualties, damage and disruption and affecting conditions for safe and sustainable return. Significant displacement, damaged infrastructure, socioeconomic deterioration and continued hostilities therefore mean that Lebanon remains in a fragile humanitarian situation.
